info.bio: Alice Cooper fue una banda de rock and roll, más en concreto hard rock, pionera del género conocido como glam rock. Surgida en 1964 en Arizona, Estados Unidos, logró su mayor auge durante los años 70. Posteriormente, su líder, continuaría como solista tomando el antiguo nombre de la banda, Alice Cooper, y moviéndose hasta nuestros días entre géneros tan dispares como el heavy metal (siendo considerado un relevante precursor de éste ), la new wave o el Pop rock

scenes.name: Hard rock americano: Aerosmith, Kiss y Alice Cooper
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: En Estados Unidos la crítica, que detesta a Black Sabbath y a Judas Priest, evita el término «heavy metal» y prefiere «hard rock», el formato radiofónico de moda en los setenta, donde caben grupos muy populares que no cumplen del todo el código: Aerosmith (1973) y Kiss (1974) son demasiado melódicos para ser heavy en esa década. Cuando el género se fragmente, el lite metal adoptará su estilo vocal melódico y sus armonías, y ambos acabarán dentro del metal ampliado. Alice Cooper, que compartía cartel con Black Sabbath, regala al heavy la estética visual de película de terror.
scenes.family: Raíces: blues rock, psicodelia y hard rock

scenes.name: Vídeos y cine: de The Song Remains the Same a Spinal Tap
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: Fuera de MTV el vídeo es un medio especializado que los fans compran: recopilaciones (Fuel for Life de Judas Priest), conciertos (Live After Death de Iron Maiden), documentales al modo de The Song Remains the Same de Led Zeppelin, cintas-revista y promociones de sellos independientes de thrash como Combat y Metal Blade. Metallica deconstruye el formato con Cliff ’em All, homenaje a Cliff Burton hecho con grabaciones caseras y piratas. El cine, que necesita un público de masas, apenas trata el metal, salvo como banda sonora de películas de terror. Las dos películas sobre él de los ochenta, This Is Spinal Tap (1984), la parodia de Rob Reiner, y The Decline of Western Civilization Part II: The Metal Years (1988) de Penelope Spheeris, dan placer al público metal pero aún más a sus detractores: una es una crítica cultural de la falta de sofisticación; la otra, una crítica moral de la depravación, estrenada tras los ataques del PMRC. Spinal Tap acabó saliendo de gira de verdad.

scenes.name: Decadencia y glam-rock
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: El rock siempre tuvo un elemento de decadencia, amoralidad y obscenidad; entre los Cockettes (1968) y el Rocky Horror Picture Show (1974) se convierte en producto de masas. Gran Bretaña lo llama glam-rock: T.Rex lo inaugura y lo casa con el hard rock; David Bowie lo lleva a su cima comercial convirtiendo el marketing en arte (Ziggy Stardust, la trilogía berlinesa con Eno). En EE UU, Alice Cooper, Sparks, Iggy Pop y Lou Reed (Berlin, Metal Machine Music, New York). El glam y la decadencia preparan el punk: Mott The Hoople, Be Bop Deluxe, New York Dolls, Heartbreakers, Dictators, Modern Lovers de Jonathan Richman, Runaways.
scenes.family: Punk, new wave, hardcore y noise

podcast.title: Chicken Incident at Toronto Rock and Roll Revival Festival (September 13, 1969)
podcast.body: At the Toronto Rock and Roll Revival Festival on September 13, 1969, Vincent Furnier, then the singer for the band Alice Cooper, threw a chicken he believed could fly into the crowd. The chicken was torn to pieces, leading to sensationalized rumors of animal sacrifice and the singer drinking its blood, which the band never denied on management's advice. "Vincent Fernier, the singer, believed that as God was his witness, chickens could fly. So he grabbed the chicken and threw it into the crowd. The chicken fell into the throng where it was torn to pieces."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Musical Influence (Post-1973)
podcast.body: Alice Cooper was among the musicians whose work Poison Ivy and Lux Interior began to "consume" after being inspired by a New York Dolls concert in 1973. This reflected their growing passion for "anything that was sexy, wild, and played rock and roll." "Esto incluía músicos como al escúper, T-Rex, Ygpop, el acetado New York Dolls."

podcast.title: Singer Adopts Band Name (1973)
podcast.body: By 1973, the band's singer, Vincent Furnier, had fully embraced the name "Alice Cooper" as his own stage persona. "By 1973, the singer, Vincent Fernier, was now being called Alice Cooper."

podcast.title: "Alice" Persona Description (1974)
podcast.body: In a 1974 interview, Alice Cooper clarified that "Alice" is a dangerous persona he cannot embody constantly. He described the band as "all American kids" who reflect America's current attitude, acting as a social mirror that can be frightening to parents. He emphasized not taking a serious standpoint or preaching, opting instead for entertainment that incorporates "hard rock" with theater, asserting that the old "jam" style of rock groups from the 60s was "dead." "Alice is a, you know, I can't be Alice all the time because he's a little bit too dangerous."

podcast.title: American Glam Rock Acceptability
podcast.body: Alice Cooper's brand of glam rock made the genre acceptable for American audiences, distinguished from British glam by its "butch manly" presentation. David Bowie noted that Cooper's use of guillotines, fireworks, muscle, and metal offered a less ambiguous sexual bent that was more readily accepted in places like Ohio, contrasting with the "snippily" British approach. "Before an apt, we were bookended by Alice and Kiss butch manly glam with lots of guillotines and fireworks, muscle and metal."

podcast.title: Gothic Appearance and Theatricality
podcast.body: Alice Cooper adopted a distinctive appearance, including makeup, gothic-type eyeliner, leather, and sometimes torn women's clothing. On stage, he assumed the role of a violent villain, incorporating elements like mock executions, snakes, fake blood, and electric chair props into his highly theatrical shows. "He wore makeup, gothic type eyeliner. He wore leather, sometimes torn off women's clothing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Horror Vibe Precursor
podcast.body: Alice Cooper's dark vibe and horror imagery were recognized as an influence on the emerging goth aesthetic, though his music was not yet considered goth itself. "People dug the dark vibe, but this wasn't goth, not yet."

podcast.title: Influence on Gothic Rock (Early 1970s)
podcast.body: Alice Cooper is credited for his influence on Gothic rock through his "death-obsessed shock rock" of the early 1970s. His theatrical and dark aesthetic paved the way for the morbid and supernatural themes prevalent in Goth music. "We also have to give Alice Cooper credit for his death-obsessed shock rock of the early 1970's."

podcast.title: Ouija Board Origin Story
podcast.body: A circulating story claimed that the name "Alice Cooper" came to Vincent Furnier during a Ouija board session, where he purportedly contacted a witch who may have been executed during the Salem Witch Trials. "And the story circulated that that name came to him as he was playing with the Ouija board, and that he had been contacted by a witch who may or may not have been executed during the Sanland Witch Trials."

podcast.title: Pioneering Theatrical Rock
podcast.body: Alice Cooper introduced a new level of theatricality to rock music, with his elaborate stage shows influencing a wide range of genres from heavy metal to art rock and industrial music. "But in the process, Alice brought a new sense of theatricality to rock. Alice worked influenced everything from heavy metal to art rock to industrial music."

xref.title: Formation and Johnny Rotten's Audition (1975)
xref.body: In 1975, Malcolm McLaren, the former manager of The New York Dolls and co-proprietor of the "Sex" clothing shop at 430 King's Road in London's Chelsea area, sought to form a band as a living advertisement for his store. He liked the name "Pistols" for its dangerous connotation, thus "Sex Pistols." Malcolm was looking for a singer and was introduced to 19-year-old Johnny Lydon (later Johnny Rotten), who had green teeth and was spotted by Bernie Rhodes wearing a homemade "I hate Pink Floyd" t-shirt held together with safety pins. Despite Lydon's inability to sing, Malcolm had him audition by miming and "singing" Alice Cooper's "I'm 18" to a jukebox in the shop, which landed him the role. "So Malcolm got young John to audition, not caring if Johnny could actually sing a note, which he couldn't."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Influences
xref.body: Pat Smear's early listening habits, before punk rock, included progressive and mainstream rock artists like Yes, Queen, Alice Cooper, and David Bowie, alongside The Runaways. He later embraced punk rock when the scene became open to bands like The Germs who "didn't know how to play." "I was listening to yes. I was listening to Queen and a Alaskupper and David Bowie."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Influences
xref.body: From childhood, Chrissie Hynde loved the guitar and, due to a scarcity of female role models, drew inspiration from James Brown's guitarist. She also admired artists like Alice Cooper, The Stooges, and Jeff Beck. "She loved the guitar from the time she was a kid. With few female role models, she looked to the guitarist employed by James Brown. She loved Alice Cooper and the stooages and Jeff Beck."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Sound Comparison
xref.body: The Germs' first proper show recording, titled "Germicide" from the summer of 1977, was perceived by guitarist Pat Smear as sounding like Alice Cooper, despite being a burgeoning punk rock act. This highlights their initial sonic aspirations before fully embracing the punk identity. "If you ever listen to the first germs recording, which is our first proper show, which is the thing, who called germicide, we think we sound like Alaskupper."

xref.body: Around his 21st birthday, Joey became deeply immersed in glam culture, idolizing David Bowie and Alice Cooper. He would dress in satin jumpsuits adorned with rhinestones and wear knee-high platform boots, which exaggerated his height to six feet eight inches. "He also became a big fan of Alice Cooper. His first real band was called Sniper."

xref.title: The Germs' Sound Self-Perception
xref.body: Pat Smear recalls that when The Germs recorded their first proper show, known as "Germicide," in the summer of 1977, the band genuinely believed they sounded like Alice Cooper, despite their raw, emerging punk sound. He challenges listeners to identify an Alice Cooper element in their early work. "we think we sound like Alaskupper. I challenge you to go listen to it and tell me what you think."
